ModelCharacter: A U.S.-built evolution of the Albin 25 concept: a rugged center-cockpit, twin-cabin family cruiser with shallow draft, full-length keel and a small single diesel capable of 10–12-knot economical coastal cruising.
DesignLineage: HMY identifies the 27 Family Cruiser as a direct descendant of the Swedish-built Albin 25.

ModelCharacter: A twin-outboard two-cabin weekender that moves the Antares concept into genuine family-cruising territory. The model now spans an original 29'11" generation and a newer Series 2 with a shorter nominal LOA but higher displacement and up to twin 250 hp.
DesignLineage: The first modern Antares 9 used a 9.12 m / 29'11" hull with twin outboards up to 200 hp each.

ModelCharacter: The larger sedan expression of Californian's LRC formula: a broad 13-foot-beam trawler-profile cruiser with wide side decks, lower helm, large cockpit and solid-fiberglass modified-V hull capable of everything from economical displacement-speed running to nearly 20-knot cruising with higher-output Caterpillar diesels.
DesignLineage: The 38 LRC Sedan was produced from 1978–1985 as the larger companion to the Californian 34 LRC.
It preserves the 34's defining combination of trawler appearance, mahogany interior, broad side decks and a modified-V hull capable of much higher speeds than conventional displacement trawlers.
Single- and twin-stateroom layouts were offered, both using a galley-up sedan arrangement and standard lower helm.
The 38 LRC Sedan should not be conflated with later Californian 38 Convertibles or Motor Yachts, which belong to different model families.
OwnershipCharacter: A strong liveaboard/coastal-cruising layout with excellent deck access and minimal exterior wood compared with many contemporaries. Twin engines, 400 gallons of fuel and 28,000 pounds of boat make it materially more expensive to own than the 34, while machinery choice can shift performance from trawler-like economy to fast-cruiser fuel consumption.

ModelCharacter: A compact high-performance expression of C. Raymond Hunt's deep-V heritage: 21-degree transom deadrise, single gasoline or diesel power, sterndrive or V-drive configurations and a finely finished weekender interior capable of 25–30-knot cruising in difficult coastal water.
DesignLineage: The Surfhunter 29 grew from Hunt's long-running Surfhunter concept and the deep-V hull form pioneered by C. Raymond Hunt.
Modern Hunt engineering refined the original concept while preserving a fine entry and approximately 21-degree transom deadrise.
Verified surviving production examples span at least 2004–2008.
Single gas and diesel packages from roughly 310–375 hp were offered with sterndrive and V-drive arrangements.
OwnershipCharacter: Premium construction and one-engine simplicity are positives, but high-output stern-drive boats demand more drivetrain maintenance than shaft-driven Downeast cruisers. Drive corrosion, bellows, transom structure, cored topsides and repower quality deserve focused survey attention.

Overview: The Sisu 22 is a Downeast/lobster-boat-derived hull whose individual finish and propulsion can vary significantly. B-Atlas treats the hull identity as useful, but not every legacy accommodation, tankage or equipment value as a factory-wide standard.

CoupleCruising.Summary: The documented layout and protected helm arrangement are practical for a cruising couple, with accommodation depth varying by model.

SoloHandling.Summary: Visibility and cockpit access are generally strong; docking burden depends on size, engine arrangement and fitted thrusters.

ModelVariations.Name: Hull-specific finishing
ModelVariations.Description: Commercial-derived Downeast hulls may be finished by different yards or owners, so house, machinery, tankage and interior arrangement require individual verification.

ModelCharacter: A Royal Lowell-designed New England classic prized for its round-chine lobsterboat hull, high bow and exceptional seaworthiness for only 22 feet. Early examples used inboard diesels; later Eastern-built versions moved to bracketed outboards while preserving both open bass-boat and lobsterboat pilothouse configurations.
DesignLineage: Royal Lowell drew the Sisu 22 in the 1970s as one of three designs for a New Hampshire builder.
After the original business failed, the molds moved among multiple builders, including production in Nova Scotia.
Eastern Boats later modernized the 22 with composite construction, recessed chines and an outboard bracket while preserving the basic Lowell hull concept.
The 22 and larger Sisu 26 are related by designer and mission but are distinct hulls.
OwnershipCharacter: Extremely simple in either single-inboard or single-outboard form, with a large open cockpit and limited hotel systems. Older examples vary dramatically by builder and finish, so hull/deck condition and the quality of any outboard conversion matter more than model-year equipment.
